# Abstract

Reconstructing long-run human population across Oceania from the terminal Pleistocene to the contemporary census era presents a distinctive methodological challenge in historical spatial demography. Spanning roughly 9,50M km² of land dispersed across more than one-third of the Earth's circumference—from the continental landmass of Sahul (Australia, Tasmania and New Guinea) through the island arcs of Near Oceania and the oceanic archipelagos of Remote Oceania—AUSTRAL bridges societies whose demographic histories diverge more sharply in chronology, ecological carrying capacity and archival density than in any other macro-region of the world. Global gridded inventories such as HYDE 3.2 [@KleinGoldewijk2017] and KK10 [@Kaplan2011], alongside classical tabular syntheses [@McEvedyJones1978], provide indispensable planetary accounting frames, yet their reliance on modern sovereign nation-state boundaries and uniform environmental suitability kernels introduces systematic spatial distortions across the Pacific. Post-colonial meridians such as the 141°E border bisecting New Guinea, the 26°S and 129°E state grids of Australia, and the sub-pixel exclusion of coral atolls routinely obscure pre-contact Indigenous watershed systems, independent highland Papuan agriculture, the late Lapita and Polynesian oceanic expansions and the sharp colonial demographic collapses of the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries.

AUSTRAL resolves these structural artefacts through an integrated bottom-up architecture comprising 16 regional and chronological chapters grouped into Pre-Colonial, Colonial and Modern Oceanic modules, backed by 310 open-access scholarly studies, 69.018 primary institutional archaeological records (with zero crowd-sourced fallback), 35.031 chapter-level settlement trajectories (26.413 chapter-distinct localities; 25.519 cross-chapter deduplicated entities and 152.483 chronological observations across 25 Oceanic territories) and 1.418 sub-administrative historical GIS enumerations spanning 14 strictly non-anachronistic territorial boundary regimes across all 118 Common Era HYDE epochs from 1AD to 2025. Pre-statistical surfaces are modelled via non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging [@PaciorekSchervish2006] across 1.554 geodesic Voronoi catchments (1.337 active domestic catchments; 86,04% coverage) conditioned on eight archaeological horizon slices from Pleistocene Sahul to early colonial contact, achieving residual variogram fits of $R^2 = 0,9927$ to $0,9993$ and an effective short correlation range of 51,8 to 58,7 km. Post-contact and contemporary rasters enforce mass-conserving pycnophylactic dasymetric scaling across period-authentic colonial and national geometries (worst unit relative error $4,44 \times 10^{-8}$), while harmonised pixel-for-pixel seam exclusions maintain exact boundary continuity against neighbouring Southeast Asian, Hawaiian and Pacific rim domains.

Across the consolidated macro-regional reconstruction (reconciling 5-arcminute gridded totals with sub-pixel Micronesian and Polynesian atoll censuses), human numbers across AUSTRAL rose from 236,4k in 10000BC and 344,7k in 6000BC to 513,1k in 1000BC following Lapita settlement of Remote Oceania and highland New Guinea agricultural intensification [@denham2003origins; @sheppard2011lapita]. By 1AD, pan-Oceanic numbers reached 2,19M—anchored by 1,23M in New Guinea and 600,4k in Australia—climbing steadily through the East Polynesian and Aotearoa New Zealand voyaging horizons to a pre-contact crest of 3,81M around 1780. Introduced pathogens, frontier dispossession and labour disruption then drove a sharp trough of 3,29M by 1820, before settler immigration across Australia and New Zealand and twentieth-century public-health transitions in New Guinea and the Pacific Islands propelled the domain to 7,43M in 1900, 13,59M in 1950, 28,20M in 1990 and 52,09M in 2025 (51,32M on the 5-arcminute continental-insular raster). Today, urban concentration across 23.964 non-suburb localities follows a tightly fitted upper-tail Zipf rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,82$, $R^2 = 0,960$), led by Sydney (5,30M), Melbourne (5,06M), Brisbane (2,57M), Perth (2,19M), Auckland (1,62M), Adelaide (1,40M) and Port Moresby (756,8k).

# Background

Long-run population reconstruction across Oceania confronts a deeper chronological and ecological asymmetry than exists in Eurasia, Africa or the Americas. Within a single oceanic theatre bounded by the Wallacean straits in the west and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in the south-east, human occupation spans more than sixty millennia in northern Sahul yet less than eight centuries in temperate Aotearoa New Zealand and extreme East Polynesia [@clarkson2017human; @bradshaw2021stochastic; @burley2012high; @matisoo_smith2026minding]. Between those two chronological poles lie four fundamentally distinct demographic trajectories: hunter-gatherer continentality across Pleistocene and Holocene Australia and Tasmania [@williams2013population; @williams2015holocene; @mulvaney2020prehistory]; an independent, high-density centre of wetland and montane tuber domestication in the Central Highlands of New Guinea [@denham2003origins; @bergstrom2017neolithic; @denham2024resonating]; the maritime Lapita and Micronesian Neolithic dispersals into Near and Remote Oceania [@sheppard2011lapita; @carson2014first; @liu2022ancient]; and the late colonial and contemporary demographic divergence between heavily urbanised settler democracies in Australia and New Zealand and rapidly growing, predominantly rural or coastal-archipelagic states in Papua New Guinea, Indonesian Papua, Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.

Existing planetary historical datasets struggle to represent these four trajectories simultaneously. Global tabular baselines [@McEvedyJones1978] and gridded Holocene land-use reconstructions [@KleinGoldewijk2017; @Kaplan2011] necessarily construct sub-continental allocation curves from modern ISO-3166 country polygons and generic biophysical suitability weights. Applied to Oceania, that design introduces four specific analytical distortions that AUSTRAL was constructed to correct.

First, projecting modern sovereign and federal borders backward across the Holocene imposes linear nineteenth-century and twentieth-century survey meridians onto Indigenous ecological territories that never followed geometric lines. In Australia, the 129°E, 138°E and 141°E meridians and the 26°S and 29°S parallels divide arid interior basins and riverine corridors—most notably the Murray-Darling system and the Lake Eyre catchment—whose pre-1788 Aboriginal populations organised around watershed resources, seasonal wetlands and ceremonial exchange networks [@tobler2017aboriginal; @crabtree2021landscape; @salles2024physiography]. In New Guinea, the 141°E colonial meridian arbitrarily slices across the trans-Fly and Digul lowlands and the central cordillera, separating linguistically and genetically linked highland horticultural populations between Indonesian Papua and Papua New Guinea [@bergstrom2017neolithic; @barker2023holocene; @denham2024resonating]. Similarly, projecting post-1989 New Zealand regional councils or post-2022 Indonesian Papuan provinces backward into the nineteenth century creates anachronistic density steps where none existed historically.

Second, generic global suitability surfaces underestimate the ecological specificity of Oceanic carrying capacity. In highland New Guinea, intensive wetland drainage at Kuk Swamp and sustained montane cultivation of taro, banana and later sweet potato supported densities exceeding 30 to 60 inhabitants/km² in intermontane valleys between 1.400 and 2.200 m elevation, whereas neighbouring malarial lowland swamps remained far more sparsely populated [@denham2003origins; @roberts2017persistent; @gonzalez_buenfil2024genetic; @denham2026clarifying]. Conversely, in continental Australia, the arid interior supported low mobile densities while coastal estuaries, mangrove littorals, the Murray-Darling basin and south-western wetlands sustained dense semi-sedentary fisheries and plant-processing economies [@florin2020first; @williams2015holocene; @norman2022human]. In Remote Oceania, island carrying capacity depended sharply on geological substrate—distinguishing fertile high volcanic islands such as Viti Levu, Upolu, Tahiti and Tongatapu from freshwater-limited coral atolls across Kiribati, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands [@rainbird2004archaeology; @field2026prey; @sear2026how].

Third, standard 5-arcminute global rasters suffer acute coastal and micro-island attenuation across the central and eastern Pacific. At the equator, a single 5-arcminute cell covers roughly 85 km², exceeding the entire emergent land area of Nauru (21 km²), Tuvalu (26 km²), Tokelau (12 km²), Pitcairn (47 km²) and individual atolls in the Marshall Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia. Standard continental land masks frequently drop low-lying atolls entirely or assign zero valid cells to Micronesia and outer Polynesia, causing gridded continental sums to understate archival island censuses by hundreds of thousands of inhabitants. Simultaneously, global grids often leak residual population into Aotearoa New Zealand and East Polynesia millennia before archaeological arrival dates—a chronological error that contradicts high-precision radiocarbon, uranium-thorium and ancient DNA chronologies [@burley2012high; @petchey2019importance; @dinapoli2021approximate; @matisoo_smith2026minding].

Fourth, settlement hierarchies across Oceania exhibit sharp municipal-versus-metropolitan boundary mismatches. In contemporary Australia, the City of Sydney local government area holds 241,8k residents inside a Greater Sydney metropolitan conurbation of 5,30M, while outer suburban councils such as Blacktown (449,4k), Casey (414,9k), Logan (403,5k) and Moreton Bay (532,4k) are statistically distinct local government units that belong functionally to the Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane metropolitan labour markets. Unreconciled compilation of city-proper, suburban-municipality and metropolitan census tables produces artificial rank-size kinks and double-counting in pan-Oceanic urban analyses.

AUSTRAL addresses each of these four weaknesses directly. By pairing watershed-based pre-colonial masking with strictly non-anachronistic colonial and national historical GIS polygons, 100% institutional archaeological provenance, dual continental-raster and atoll-reconciled population series, and three-phase metropolitan reconciliation, AUSTRAL supplies a transparent spatial-demographic synthesis aligned cleanly at its western and north-eastern oceanic seams with neighbouring regional studies.

# Methodology

## Macro-Regional Scope, Seam Exclusions and 16-Chapter Architecture

AUSTRAL encompasses a consolidated terrestrial footprint of 9,50M km² in its contemporary administrative configuration (9,46M km² in its pre-colonial watershed partition), spanning Australia, Tasmania, Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island; Aotearoa New Zealand and the Chatham Islands; the entire island of New Guinea (both Papua New Guinea and Indonesian West New Guinea including Raja Ampat) together with the Bismarck Archipelago; Island Melanesia (Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji including Rotuma); Micronesia (Palau, Federated States of Micronesia, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, Marshall Islands, Kiribati and Nauru); and Polynesia excluding Hawai'i and American Samoa (Independent Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, Cook Islands, Niue, Tuvalu, Tokelau, Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn Islands and Rapa Nui).

To prevent double-counting or boundary gaps during global compositing across adjacent macro-regions, AUSTRAL enforces three explicit pixel-for-pixel seam exclusions on the shared 4320x2160 equirectangular 5-arcminute reference grid. Along the western Wallacean seam, the Southeast Asian MANDALA domain mask is subtracted pixel-for-pixel, excluding Maluku (Gebe, East Seram, Babar, Tanimbar, Kai and Aru) and all landmasses west of 129,5°E north of 11,3°S while retaining Raja Ampat and the Bird's Head peninsula within New Guinea. Along the central and north-eastern Pacific seam, the CENTAUR Hawaiian and American Samoan mask is subtracted pixel-for-pixel, excluding the Hawaiian archipelago, Palmyra Atoll and American Samoa east of 171,25°W while preserving the eastern tip of Upolu in Independent Samoa at 171,44°W. Along the northern and far-eastern maritime margins, Japanese Bonin and Volcano islands (north of 21°N between 129,5°E and 160°E) and Clipperton and Mexican Pacific islands (north of 9,5°N between 116°W and 105°W) are excluded to match East Asian and Mesoamerican domains. All Pacific-spanning polygons—notably Fiji, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Tonga and the Chatham Islands—are projected using antimeridian-safe wrapped geometries so that no 180° meridian spikes or scanline tears enter either the areal masks or cartographic outputs.

The macro-region is partitioned into 16 thematic chapters organised into three chronological epochs (Table 1 and Figure 1): five Pre-Colonial chapters (Chapters 1 to 5), six Colonial chapters (Chapters 6 to 11) and five Modern census-era chapters (Chapters 12 to 16). Rather than imposing a uniform transition year across the Pacific, epoch transitions respect authentic regional historical thresholds: 1788 and 1901 in Australia (First Fleet and Federation); 1840 and 1907 in New Zealand (Treaty of Waitangi and Dominion status); 1884 and 1962/1975 in New Guinea (imperial partition, West New Guinea transfer and Papua New Guinea independence); 1850 and 1960/1970 in Island Melanesia; 1668 and 1960/1979 in Micronesia (beginning with Spanish colonisation of the Mariana Islands); and 1800 and 1960/1962 in Polynesia. Each chapter comprises a standalone literature review, an evidence-only settlement gazetteer, a coordinate-anchored machine-readable trajectory archive, a 4320x2160 areal mask, a matched vector regional partition and an archival library of 18 to 20 open-access scholarly PDFs (310 archival PDFs in total).

```{r tab-chapters, results='asis'}
ch_list <- root_summary$chapters
df_ch <- data.frame(
  Ch = sapply(ch_list, function(x) sprintf("%02d", as.integer(x$index))),
  Module = sapply(ch_list, function(x) x$title),
  Span = sapply(ch_list, function(x) {
    d0 <- as.integer(x$domain[[1]])
    d1 <- as.integer(x$domain[[2]])
    s0 <- if (d0 < 0) paste0(abs(d0), "BC") else as.character(d0)
    s1 <- if (d1 < 0) paste0(abs(d1), "BC") else as.character(d1)
    paste0(s0, "-", s1)
  }),
  Area_km2 = sapply(ch_list, function(x) viscount_fmt_pop(x$area_km2)),
  Zones = sapply(ch_list, function(x) as.character(x$subregions)),
  Setts = sapply(ch_list, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$settlements), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  HGIS = sapply(ch_list, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$hgis_rows), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_ch) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_ch,
  "Canonical 16-chapter itinerary of AUSTRAL showing chronological spans, equal-area footprints, regional partitions, settlement trajectories and historical GIS sub-administrative rows.",
  c("Ch.", "Regional and Chronological Module", "Span", "Area (km²)", "Zones", "Setts", "HGIS"),
  list(label = "tab:austral-chapters", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Non-Anachronistic Areal Masks and 14-Regime Historical GIS Stack

All 16 chapter masks and all 118 Common Era sub-administrative boundary rasters follow a strict five-tier provenance hierarchy: official national and academic historical GIS polygons ($z = 5$, including Australian Bureau of Statistics ASGS and Esri Historical Australian Colonies, Statistics New Zealand regional councils and Te Puni Kōkiri iwi rohe, HDX COD-AB Papua New Guinea provinces, BPS Indonesian Papua six-province boundaries and national Pacific ADM1 geometries); OpenHistoricalMap historical polities ($z = 4$); CShapes colonial and post-colonial territories ($z = 3$); coastal-matched de jure historical atlases ($z = 2$); and de facto fallbacks ($z = 1$) strictly restricted to unmapped frontiers. Pre-colonial chapters (Chapters 1, 2 and 5) replace straight colonial borders entirely with organic HydroBASINS Level-5 and Level-6 river catchments—11 ecological basins across mainland Australia and Tasmania, nine watershed zones bridging the 141°E meridian across New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago, and seven North and South Island watershed regions across Aotearoa New Zealand.

Across the 118 Common Era HYDE time steps from 1AD to 2025, AUSTRAL deploys 14 distinct historical boundary regimes totalling 1.418 sub-administrative census rows across 25 jurisdictions. Every territorial boundary transition is anchored to its actual historical date: from 1AD through 1780, all 56 units represent pre-colonial Indigenous watersheds and island polities; the 1790–1820 regime introduces New South Wales and Van Diemen's Land east of 135°E against New Holland to the west (49 units); the 1830 and 1840–1850 regimes register the Swan River Colony (Western Australia west of 129°E) and South Australia (132°E to 141°E south of 26°S, 51 to 56 units); the 1860 and 1870–1880 regimes reflect the six pre-Federation Australian colonies (including New South Wales's 1859–1863 Northern Territory exclave and South Australia's 1863–1910 administration of the Northern Territory) alongside New Zealand's ten 1853–1876 provinces (59 to 61 units); the 1890–1910 regimes introduce the tri-colonial partition of New Guinea into Dutch West New Guinea, German Kaiser-Wilhelmsland and the Bismarcks, and British-Australian Papua (56 units); the 1920–1950 and 1951–1959 regimes separate the Australian Northern Territory and Capital Territory after 1911 and track League of Nations and United Nations trusteeships (57 to 62 units); the 1960–1962 and 1963–2002 regimes retain a unified West New Guinea province west of 141°E alongside post-war Pacific and provincial divisions (107 units); the 2003–2021 regime reflects Indonesia's two-province Papuan split (Papua and Papua Barat, 107 units); and only the 2022–2025 regime introduces Indonesia's six post-2022 Papuan provinces alongside all 22 Papua New Guinea provinces, nine Australian states and territories, 17 New Zealand regions and 56 Pacific ADM1 units (110 units in total).

## Institutional Archaeological Corpora and Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging

Pre-statistical spatial surfaces from 10000BC through early colonial contact are anchored to 69.018 unique primary institutional archaeological sites consolidated into 39.897 deduplicated domestic site complexes across four macro-jurisdictions (Table 2). In contrast to projects that must lean on crowd-sourced gazetteers to fill regional gaps, AUSTRAL achieves 100,0% primary institutional and scholarly provenance with 0,0% crowd-sourced fallback across all four jurisdictions.

In Australia (49.176 sites; 42.528 habitation sites and 6.648 monument-only sites), institutional records combine the AustArch and SahulArch OCTOPUS v2 radiocarbon compendia (2.311 radiocarbon-anchored sites) with state and commonwealth statutory heritage registers: Western Australia DPLH Aboriginal Cultural Heritage lodged and registered corpora (33.026 combined records), the Victorian Heritage Inventory (7.161 records), South Australia Heritage Places (2.290), New South Wales State Heritage and Aboriginal Places registers (1.852), Queensland Heritage and Aboriginal Cultural Heritage registers (1.549), the Tasmanian Heritage Register (577) and Commonwealth and National Heritage lists (410) [@williams2013population; @williams2015holocene; @clarkson2017human]. In Aotearoa New Zealand (16.668 sites; 16.417 habitation sites), primary records integrate the Waikato Aotearoa New Zealand Radiocarbon Database (2.031 sites), NZAA ArchSite regional extractions (9.453 sites across Far North, Gisborne, Pokeno, Oturu and Bay of Plenty), LINZ 1:50k fortified *pā* earthworks (2.144 sites), Te Puni Kōkiri *marae* locations (892), Environment Canterbury and Ngāi Tahu cultural site registers (1.167), Nelson-Tasman and Waikato heritage registers (590) and Prickett's New Zealand Wars fortification corpus (391).

Across New Guinea and Island Melanesia (1.400 sites; 1.395 habitation sites) and Polynesia and Micronesia (1.774 sites; 1.359 habitation sites), where national digital heritage portals are far scarcer, AUSTRAL integrates pan-Pacific archaeological databases: the Pacific Archaeological Radiocarbon Database PARD 2025 (1.385 sites), the Pofatu geochemical artefact database (662 sites), the ANU Kuden Lapita and post-Lapita pottery corpus (272 sites), French Polynesia's Te Fenua heritage inventory (306 sites), the US National Park Service NRHP Micronesian register (86 sites), the Easter Island Statue Project *ahu* register (73 sites), Harvard AADR v66 ancient DNA localities (35 sites), the Academia Sinica Lapita Pottery Online Database (16 sites) and New Caledonia Province Sud heritage records [@summerhayes2010human; @sheppard2011lapita; @lipson2018population; @lipo2025megalithic].

```{r tab-arch-prov, results='asis'}
ap <- root_summary$archaeological_provenance$jurisdiction_arch_coverage
j_keys <- c("australia", "new_zealand", "new_guinea_melanesia", "polynesia_micronesia")
j_labels <- c("Australia and Tasmania", "Aotearoa New Zealand", "New Guinea and Melanesia", "Polynesia and Micronesia")
fmt_int <- function(v) formatC(as.integer(v), format = "d", big.mark = ".")

df_ap <- data.frame(
  Jurisdiction = j_labels,
  Total = sapply(j_keys, function(k) fmt_int(ap[[k]]$total_sites)),
  Registers = sapply(j_keys, function(k) fmt_int(ap[[k]]$regional_register_sites)),
  Monographs = sapply(j_keys, function(k) fmt_int(ap[[k]]$monograph_sites)),
  Radiocarbon = sapply(j_keys, function(k) fmt_int(ap[[k]]$c14_primary_sites)),
  Habitation = sapply(j_keys, function(k) fmt_int(ap[[k]]$habitation_sites)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
tot_row <- data.frame(
  Jurisdiction = "AUSTRAL Total",
  Total = fmt_int(sum(sapply(j_keys, function(k) ap[[k]]$total_sites))),
  Registers = fmt_int(sum(sapply(j_keys, function(k) ap[[k]]$regional_register_sites))),
  Monographs = fmt_int(sum(sapply(j_keys, function(k) ap[[k]]$monograph_sites))),
  Radiocarbon = fmt_int(sum(sapply(j_keys, function(k) ap[[k]]$c14_primary_sites))),
  Habitation = fmt_int(sum(sapply(j_keys, function(k) ap[[k]]$habitation_sites))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_ap <- rbind(df_ap, tot_row)
rownames(df_ap) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_ap,
  "Primary institutional archaeological site provenance across the four Oceanic macro-jurisdictions (zero crowd-sourced fallback in every jurisdiction).",
  c("Macro-Jurisdiction", "Total Sites", "Registers", "Monographs", "Radiocarbon", "Habitation"),
  list(label = "tab:arch-provenance", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

These archaeological records are partitioned into eight chronological horizon layers spanning the Holocene: (1) Pleistocene and Early Holocene Sahul (911 sites, 918 active catchments), (2) Mid-Holocene Intensification and Kuk Swamp agriculture (1.716 sites, 990 catchments), (3) Lapita and Austronesian dispersal (2.228 sites, 1.012 catchments), (4) Post-Lapita Melanesian and West Polynesian consolidation (2.509 sites, 1.031 catchments), (5) Central and East Polynesian expansion (2.562 sites, 1.125 catchments), (6) Aotearoa settlement and classic Pacific chiefdoms (2.450 sites, 1.161 catchments), (7) Classic Māori *pā* and late pre-contact polities (2.828 sites, 1.123 catchments), and (8) Contact and early colonial transition (5.982 sites, 1.231 catchments).

To translate discrete archaeological point clusters into continuous 5-arcminute population density priors without over-smoothing sharp coastal-interior gradients, AUSTRAL implements non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging over 1.554 geodesic Voronoi catchments (median radius 33,1 km, 90th-percentile radius 53,9 km) [@PaciorekSchervish2006]. The local site-density log-intensity $Z(s)$ at cell $s$ is decomposed into a weighted least-squares biophysical trend plus a spatially correlated zero-mean Gaussian field:

$$Z(s) = \beta_0 H(s) + \beta_1 N(s) + \beta_2 E(s) + \beta_3 F(s) + \beta_4 C(s) + \varepsilon(s)$$

where $H(s)$ denotes composite habitability, $N(s)$ natural vegetation productivity, $E(s)$ ecological suitability, $F(s)$ fluvial proximity and $C(s)$ coastal littoral accessibility, and $\varepsilon(s)$ follows a two-component Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) covariance kernel with nugget ratio $\eta$ and dimensionless range parameters $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ scaled to local Voronoi catchment geometry:

$$\gamma(u) = c_0 + c_1 \left[1 - \left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_1}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_1}\right)\right] + c_2 \left[1 - \left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_2}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_2}\right)\right]$$

with structural weights fixed at $c_1 = 0,80$ and $c_2 = 0,20$ and regularised correlation ranges $\tau_1 = 1,35$ and $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (Table 3). Within every post-contact administrative polygon, final cell counts are generated by pycnophylactic dasymetric scaling that multiplies the kriged environmental suitability prior by an exact unit-level normalising factor so that cell sums equal recorded archival enumerations to machine precision.

```{r tab-variogram, results='asis'}
vm <- root_summary$kriging_diagnostics$variogram_models
pg <- root_summary$archaeological_provenance$period_geojsons
p_labels <- c(
  "01_pleistocene_early_holocene_sahul" = "1. Pleistocene-Early Holocene Sahul",
  "02_mid_holocene_intensification_kuk" = "2. Mid-Holocene Intensification & Kuk",
  "03_lapita_austronesian_dispersal" = "3. Lapita & Austronesian Dispersal",
  "04_post_lapita_melanesian_west_polynesia" = "4. Post-Lapita & West Polynesia",
  "05_central_east_polynesia_expansion" = "5. Central-East Polynesia Expansion",
  "06_aotearoa_settlement_classic_chiefdoms" = "6. Aotearoa Settlement & Chiefdoms",
  "07_classic_maori_pa_pacific_polities" = "7. Classic Maori Pa & Pacific Polities",
  "08_contact_and_early_colonial_transition" = "8. Contact & Early Colonial Transition"
)
df_vm <- data.frame(
  Horizon = sapply(pg, function(x) unname(p_labels[x$key])),
  Sites = sapply(pg, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$total_sites_count), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  Catchments = sapply(pg, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$active_domestic_catchments), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  Range_km = sapply(pg, function(x) viscount_fmt_number(vm[[x$key]]$effective_short_range_km, 2)),
  Fluvial_b = sapply(pg, function(x) viscount_fmt_number(vm[[x$key]]$residual_kriging_wls_betas$beta_3_fluvial, 4)),
  Coastal_b = sapply(pg, function(x) viscount_fmt_number(vm[[x$key]]$residual_kriging_wls_betas$beta_4_coastal, 4)),
  R2 = sapply(pg, function(x) viscount_fmt_number(vm[[x$key]]$residual_r2, 4)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_vm) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_vm,
  "Non-stationary Matérn (nu = 3/2) variogram and weighted least-squares trend parameters across the eight archaeological horizon slices of AUSTRAL.",
  c("Archaeological Horizon", "Sites", "Catch.", "Range (km)", "Fluvial b3", "Coastal b4", "Residual R²"),
  list(label = "tab:variogram-matern", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Evidence-Only Settlement Gazetteers and Three-Phase Metropolitan Reconciliation

Across all 16 chapters, settlement gazetteers were assembled strictly from documentary, archaeological and official statistical evidence—excluding synthetic placeholder centroids, unreferenced gazetteer dumps and invented back-projections. Pre-colonial settlements draw on radiocarbon-dated residential complexes, fortified *pā*, ceremonial *ahu* and *marae* clusters, and ethnohistorical contact villages across Australia, New Guinea, Island Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia. Colonial gazetteers digitise early colonial musters, colonial statistical registers, gold-rush township enumerations, missionary island counts and colonial administrative reports for Australia (1788–1901), New Zealand (1840–1907), New Guinea (1884–1975), Island Melanesia (1850–1970), Micronesia (1668–1979) and Polynesia (1800–1962). Contemporary gazetteers ingest Australian Bureau of Statistics Urban Centres and Localities (UCL), Suburbs and Localities (SAL) and Local Government Area time series, Statistics New Zealand census meshblock, area-unit and urban-area series, Papua New Guinea NSO ward/LLG and Indonesian BPS distrik censuses, and national statistical office enumerations across all 25 territories—yielding 35.031 chapter settlement trajectories, 26.413 unique chapter-distinct localities (25.519 cross-chapter deduplicated entities) and 152.483 chronological observations.

To eliminate city-proper versus metropolitan distortion in pan-Oceanic urban analysis, AUSTRAL applies a structured three-phase metropolitan reconciliation protocol. In Phase 1, every locality is classified explicitly by statistical scope into metropolitan statistical areas (55 metros across Oceania), standalone cities, towns and rural villages (23.909 city-proper localities spanning all 25 territories) and constituent suburban local government councils and outer-suburban localities (2.449 suburban units embedded within larger Australian and New Zealand conurbations). In Phase 2, constituent suburban units (such as Blacktown, Parramatta, Canterbury-Bankstown, Northern Beaches, Liverpool and Cumberland inside Greater Sydney; Casey, Wyndham, Hume and Whittlesea inside Greater Melbourne; Moreton Bay, Logan and Ipswich inside Greater Brisbane; and Stirling and Wanneroo inside Greater Perth) are tagged as subordinate suburban scopes so they are preserved for intra-metropolitan analysis yet excluded from pan-Oceanic rank-size and Zipf regressions. In Phase 3, core city-proper units are linked to their parent metropolitan statistical envelopes while preventing double-counting across overlapping chapter boundaries, producing a clean set of 23.964 unique non-suburb localities for pan-Oceanic Zipf estimation.

# Testing and Validation

Quantitative quality assurance across AUSTRAL spans four independent pillars: archaeological variogram and kriging diagnostics, pycnophylactic HGIS mass conservation, visual mask and seam-exclusion audits, and pan-Oceanic settlement and Zipf hierarchy checks (Table 4 and Figure 2).

First, across all eight archaeological horizon slices (117.888 valid terrestrial cells on the 5-arcminute grid, 63.696 active kriged cells, 1.337 active domestic catchments out of 1.554 Voronoi units), the non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) variogram model achieves residual fits between $R^2 = 0,9927$ (Classic Māori *pā* and Pacific Polities) and $R^2 = 0,9993$ (Pleistocene and Early Holocene Sahul). Effective short correlation ranges remain tightly bounded between 51,82 km and 58,71 km, tracking the mesoscale spacing of riverine valleys, coastal estuaries and island clusters. Weighted least-squares trend coefficients confirm expected ecological mechanics: composite habitability ($\beta_0$) declines gradually from 0,2130 in Pleistocene Sahul to 0,0806–0,0827 in late pre-contact and contact horizons as agricultural intensification and maritime voyaging decoupled human settlement from raw foraging productivity, while fluvial ($\beta_3 = 0,0928$–$0,1089$) and coastal ($\beta_4 = 0,0626$–$0,0938$) weights remain consistently positive across every horizon (Figure 2, Panel A). Comparing kriged pre-statistical priors against HYDE 3.2 yields a moderate log-density correlation of $0,5018$ (with urban core median ratio $0,7881$ and urban back-projection 95th-percentile ratio $1,286$)—precisely the expected divergence where primary institutional archaeological registers (69.018 sites with 0,0% crowd fallback; Figure 2, Panel B) redirect mass away from HYDE's generic continental smoothers toward documented highland Papuan valleys, coastal Australian shell-midden belts and northern Aotearoa *pā* concentrations.

```{r fig2-krige, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/02_austral_kriging_diagnostics.png",
  "Non-stationary Matérn (nu = 3/2) sample variogram curves across four archaeological horizons (Panel A) and institutional archaeological site provenance across the four Oceanic macro-jurisdictions (Panel B).",
  "fig:kriging-diag"
)
```

Second, automated mass-conservation verification across all 118 Common Era sub-administrative HGIS rasters (spanning 14 non-anachronistic boundary regimes from 1AD to 2025) confirms exact pycnophylactic fidelity: the worst relative discrepancy across every administrative unit in every scaled year is $4,44 \times 10^{-8}$, and the worst territory-level relative discrepancy is $2,20 \times 10^{-8}$, both more than four orders of magnitude tighter than the $1,0 \times 10^{-3}$ tolerance ceiling. Independent visual cartographic inspection signed off all 16 chapter masks and all eight benchmark sub-administrative regime crops (1700, 1800, 1840, 1860, 1890, 1910, 1960 and 2025) at 100% land coverage, verifying the removal of stray coastal slivers in 1800 Western Australia, spurious 135°E strips in 1840 Australia, interior sliver artefacts in 1890–1910 Papua, anachronistic pre-2003 West New Guinea splits in 1960, and Kiribati Phoenix Islands coordinate displacement.

Third, cross-regional seam audits confirm zero pixel overlap against neighbouring Southeast Asian, Hawaiian and Pacific rim masks, alongside zero antimeridian polygon tearing across 180°E in Fiji, Kiribati, Tonga, Tuvalu and the Chatham Islands.

Fourth, settlement hierarchy diagnostics verify the statistical impact of three-phase metropolitan reconciliation. When raw suburban units (2.449 units) are pooled indiscriminately with metropolitan statistical areas (55 units) and standalone cities and villages (23.909 units) across all 26.413 unique localities, the upper-tail Zipf exponent ($n = 180$) is depressed artificially to $\alpha = 0,747$ ($R^2 = 0,9800$) because massive Australian outer-suburban councils crowd ranks 10 through 50. Removing subordinate suburban units raises the upper-tail fit across the 23.964 non-suburb localities to $\alpha = 0,823$ with $R^2 = 0,9601$ (full-sample slope $-1,4941$, $R^2 = 0,8920$).

# Results

## Long-Run Holocene Demographic Trajectory (10000BC–2025)

Consolidated pan-Oceanic population totals trace five broad demographic phases between the terminal Pleistocene and 2025 (Figure 3, Table 5 and Table 6). At 10000BC, immediately following post-glacial sea-level rise that drowned the Carpentaria plain and began severing Tasmania and New Guinea from mainland Australia, AUSTRAL held an estimated 236,4k inhabitants in the reconciled series (241,1k on the raw 5-arcminute raster)—nearly 87% located across Aboriginal Australia and Tasmania (206,3k), alongside 27,8k in New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago and 2,4k in Near Oceanic Island Melanesia, while Micronesia, Polynesia and Aotearoa New Zealand remained uninhabited. This baseline sits within the genetic and stochastic-demographic envelope established for Late Pleistocene and early Holocene Sahul following deliberate maritime crossings through Wallacea around 65.000 to 50.000 years ago [@clarkson2017human; @bird2019early; @bradshaw2021stochastic; @salles2024physiography; @shipton2024abrupt; @gandini2025genomic].

During the Early and Mid-Holocene (10000BC–2000BC), continental and insular trajectories diverged sharply. Across Australia, radiocarbon summed probability distributions, regional mitogenomic structure and inland archaeobotanical records indicate modest early Holocene growth to 299,3k around 6000BC, a mid-Holocene reorganisation amid arid-zone El Niño intensification (165,7k at 4000BC and 227,1k at 3000BC), and subsequent late Holocene intensification across riverine and coastal fisheries lifting Aboriginal numbers to 326,5k by 1000BC [@williams2013population; @williams2015holocene; @malaspinas2016genomic; @tobler2017aboriginal; @florin2021pandanus; @david2024archaeologic]. Concurrently, in the New Guinea Highlands, persistent montane plant exploitation documented from 49.000 years ago at Ivane Valley evolved into independent wetland mounding and drainage agriculture at Kuk Swamp by 10.000 to 7.000 cal BP [@summerhayes2010human; @denham2003origins; @anonymous2017ten; @horrocks2025palaeoecolog; @denham2026clarifying]. Highland taro, banana and yam cultivation drove a sustained Neolithic demographic expansion that lifted New Guinea from 27,8k in 10000BC and 42,5k in 6000BC to 53,8k by 2000BC and 93,7k by 1000BC, while strong topographic isolation preserved deep regional genetic differentiation across highlands and lowlands [@bergstrom2017neolithic; @barker2023holocene; @quinn2024population].

```{r fig3-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/03_austral_secular_trajectory.png",
  "Secular demographic trajectories of AUSTRAL macro-regions from 10000BC to 2025 on semi-logarithmic scale (Panel A) and post-1780 colonial-to-modern linear scale (Panel B).",
  "fig:secular-traj"
)
```

The second millennium BC opened Remote Oceania to human habitation through two distinct Austronesian voyaging pulses. Around 2000BC–1500BC, seafarers from the northern Philippines crossed the Philippine Sea to settle the Mariana Islands (Saipan, Tinian and Guam), establishing early Micronesian communities represented by 48,5k inhabitants at 2000BC and 52,0k at 1000BC in the reconciled series [@clark2009radiocarbon; @carson2014first; @pugach2020ancient; @liu2022ancient]. Shortly thereafter, around 1500BC–1000BC, the Lapita Cultural Complex emerged in the Bismarck Archipelago—anchored by early dentate-stamped pottery sites such as Tamuarawai on Emirau Island and obsidian exchange networks extending from West New Britain across the Southwest Pacific—before leapfrogging the Near-Remote Oceania boundary into Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries [@torrence2004pleistocene; @summerhayes2009tamuarawai; @sheppard2011lapita; @cochrane2018evolution; @hogg2024lapita; @ono2025early]. These maritime dispersals lifted reconciled pan-Oceanic population to 513,1k by 1000BC, including 35,7k in founder West Polynesian archipelagos (Tonga and Samoa) documented at Nukuleka and Mulifanua [@petchey2001radiocarbon; @burley2010nukuleka; @burley2012high; @petchey2019importance].

Between 1AD and 1780, agricultural intensification across New Guinea, Melanesia and the Pacific Islands combined with the final settlement of East Polynesia and Aotearoa New Zealand to raise reconciled AUSTRAL population from 2,19M in 1AD to 2,97M in 1000AD, 3,54M in 1500AD and a pre-contact crest of 3,81M around 1780 (Table 5). New Guinea remained the demographic heavyweight of pre-colonial Oceania throughout the Common Era, expanding from 1,23M in 1AD to 1,73M in 1000AD and 2,20M by 1780—over half of the entire macro-region—augmented after c. 1600AD by the rapid highland adoption of the sweet potato (*Ipomoea batatas*), which raised carrying capacity in higher-altitude Enga, Wahgi and Baliem valleys [@denham2024resonating; @barker2025marine]. Australia rose gradually from 600,4k in 1AD to 784,3k on the eve of British landing at Port Jackson in 1788, consistent with modern archaeological and economic-demographic revisions of L. R. Smith and N. G. Butlin's contact benchmarks [@anon1984aboriginal; @thornton1986our; @hunter2015estimating]. Island Melanesia grew from 213,0k in 1AD to 421,8k by 1780 following post-Lapita population turnover and intensive inland taro-pondfield terracing across Fiji, Vanuatu and New Caledonia [@anderson2009faunal; @kinaston2014lapita; @lipson2018population; @posth2018language; @hawkins2026vanuatu].

In Micronesia, reconciled totals climbed from 84,5k in 1AD to a pre-contact peak of 159,0k around 1600AD across Palau, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, the Marianas, the Marshalls and Kiribati before Spanish conquest and epidemic mortality in the Mariana Islands after 1668 initiated a sharp regional decline to 92,8k by 1780 [@rainbird2004archaeology; @fitzpatrick2010critique; @nunn2010defending]. Across Polynesia, climate-assisted eastward voyaging settled the Society, Marquesas, Cook, Austral and Mangareva archipelagos as well as Rapa Nui and Aotearoa New Zealand between c. 900AD and 1300AD [@sear2026how; @kahn2026morphologica; @dinapoli2021approximate; @lipo2025megalithic; @matisoo_smith2026minding]. Reconciled Polynesian numbers (excluding Hawai'i and American Samoa) tripled from 65,2k in 1AD to 209,3k by 1500AD and 213,6k in 1780, while Aotearoa New Zealand expanded rapidly from small East Polynesian founder colonies (239 in the 700AD early-window baseline and 410 at 1200AD before accelerating sharply after c. 1250–1300AD) to 18,0k by 1400AD, 43,1k by 1500AD and 96,6k in 1780 across fortified *pā* landscapes and kūmara gardens centred on Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and East Coast [@hingston2015phylogeograp; @matisoo_smith2026minding].

```{r tab-macro-secular, results='asis'}
mr <- root_summary$macro_reconciled_series
sel_yrs <- c("-10000", "-6000", "-3000", "-1000", "0", "1000", "1500", "1780", "1800", "1850", "1900", "1950", "1970", "1990", "2010", "2025")
fmt_yr <- function(y) {
  yi <- as.integer(y)
  if (yi < 0) paste0(abs(yi), "BC") else if (yi == 0) "1AD" else if (yi <= 1500) paste0(yi, "AD") else as.character(yi)
}
fmt_cell <- function(v) {
  val <- as.numeric(v)
  if (is.na(val) || val == 0) return("0")
  viscount_fmt_pop(val)
}

df_sec <- data.frame(
  Year = sapply(sel_yrs, fmt_yr),
  Australia = sapply(sel_yrs, function(y) fmt_cell(mr$australia[[y]])),
  New_Zealand = sapply(sel_yrs, function(y) fmt_cell(mr$new_zealand[[y]])),
  New_Guinea = sapply(sel_yrs, function(y) fmt_cell(mr$new_guinea[[y]])),
  Island_Melanesia = sapply(sel_yrs, function(y) fmt_cell(mr$island_melanesia[[y]])),
  Micronesia = sapply(sel_yrs, function(y) fmt_cell(mr$micronesia[[y]])),
  Polynesia = sapply(sel_yrs, function(y) fmt_cell(mr$polynesia[[y]])),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_sec) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_sec,
  "Reconciled secular population trajectories across the six macro-regions of AUSTRAL from 10000BC to 2025 (excluding Hawai'i and American Samoa).",
  c("Year", "Australia", "New Zealand", "New Guinea", "Isl. Melanesia", "Micronesia", "Polynesia"),
  list(label = "tab:macro-secular", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Colonial Demographic Collapse and Settler-Colony Divergence (1788–1945)

Between 1788 and the early twentieth century, AUSTRAL experienced one of the most stark demographic bifurcations in global history: catastrophic Indigenous depopulation from virgin-soil epidemics, frontier violence and dispossession unfolding simultaneously alongside rapid European settler expansion in temperate Australia and New Zealand (Figure 3, Panel B).

In Australia, the 1789 smallpox (or varicella-smallpox complex) outbreak at Port Jackson, subsequent waves across the Murray-Darling basin in the 1820s and 1830s, and pastoral frontier conflict drove continental population down from 784,3k in 1780 to a nadir of 274,7k by 1820—before British convict transportation, pastoral expansion and the 1851 Victorian and New South Wales gold rushes inverted the trajectory entirely [@thornton1986our; @hunter2015estimating; @burke2013archaeology]. Australian population surged from 399,0k in 1840 and 600,3k in 1850 to 1,33M in 1860, 2,37M in 1880 and 3,86M on the eve of Federation in 1900 (reaching 3,92M in Chapter 6 by 1901). Aotearoa New Zealand followed a compressed parallel arc: introduced respiratory infections, measles and Musket Wars cut Māori numbers from 96,6k in 1780 to 86,3k at the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi (and a Māori nadir near 42k in the 1896 census), while organised British settlement and Otago-Westland gold rushes pushed combined New Zealand totals from 89,3k in 1850 to 312,8k in 1870, 604,0k in 1890 and 812,8k in 1900.

Across tropical Oceania, where settler immigration remained minor outside New Caledonia and Fiji's indentured Indo-Fijian plantation workforce, demographic contraction lasted far longer. In Polynesia, dysentery, measles, smallpox, tuberculosis and Peruvian slave raids on Rapa Nui and Tokelau slashed reconciled totals by more than half, from 213,9k in 1800 to 137,0k in 1850 and a trough of 104,6k around 1890 (with French Polynesia, the Marquesas, Cook Islands and Rapa Nui suffering acute local collapses before slow twentieth-century recovery) [@dinapoli2021approximate; @spriggs2017thomas]. Micronesia bottomed out at 82,7k around 1850—down nearly 48% from its 1600AD peak—before Japanese Mandate sugar-and-phosphate migration to Saipan, Tinian, Palau and Nauru lifted Micronesian numbers to 129,9k in 1930 and 147,6k in 1940, shortly before Second World War combat devastated the Marianas, Peleliu, Chuuk and Tarawa. Island Melanesia contracted from 440,1k in 1850 to a trough of 353,1k around 1920 under the combined toll of the 1875 Fijian measles epidemic, *blackbirding* labour recruitment in Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands, and colonial land alienation in New Caledonia, even as Indo-Fijian indenture began reshaping Fiji's ethnic and spatial demography. In New Guinea, coastal contact epidemics and plantation recruitment nudged totals gently downward from 2,27M in 1880 to 2,14M in 1920, yet the vast interior Highlands—containing roughly one million cultivators—remained largely insulated from direct colonial contact until the 1930s patrols [@denham2024resonating; @quinn2024population].

Taken together, pan-Oceanic population dipped from 3,81M in 1780 to 3,29M in 1820, recovered past its pre-contact level only in the late 1850s (4,36M in 1860), and then climbed rapidly to 7,43M in 1900, 9,49M in 1920 and 11,74M in 1940—by which date Australia (7,16M) and New Zealand (1,65M) accounted for 75,0% of the entire macro-region, reversing their 23,1% pre-contact share in 1780.

## Post-War Public-Health Transition and Contemporary Redistribution (1945–2025)

Between 1950 and 2025, reconciled AUSTRAL population nearly quadrupled from 13,59M to 52,09M, driven by two structurally distinct growth engines: sustained post-war European and Asian immigration into Australia and New Zealand, and high-fertility public-health transitions across New Guinea and Island Melanesia (Table 5 and Table 6).

Australia expanded more than threefold from 8,40M in 1950 to 12,81M in 1970, 17,17M in 1990 and 27,79M in 2025, propelled by post-war assisted migration, the post-1973 dismantling of racially selective immigration policies and twenty-first-century skilled and student inflows concentrated heavily along the south-eastern coastal arc from Brisbane to Melbourne plus Perth. New Zealand grew from 1,95M in 1950 to 3,35M in 1990 and 5,10M in 2025, marked by rapid post-war Māori urban migration, substantial Pacific Islander immigration into Auckland and late-twentieth-century diversification toward Asian and global migration streams—shifting the country's demographic gravity steadily northward toward the Auckland-Waikato-Bay of Plenty golden triangle.

Yet the fastest proportional expansion since 1950 occurred in New Guinea. Antibiotics, malaria control, highway construction across the Highlands and rapid fertility retention propelled combined Papua New Guinea and Indonesian Papua totals from 2,29M in 1950 to 3,41M in 1970, 5,50M in 1990, 12,57M in 2010 and 16,03M in 2025 (with Chapter 14 documenting 15,64M across official provincial census baselines and 17,61M at the 2020 peak-enumeration reconciliation before recent census-base harmonisation). In western New Guinea, Indonesian *transmigrasi* programmes and resource extraction around Timika, Sorong, Jayapura and Merauke reshaped coastal and lowland densities alongside resilient Indigenous highland populations in Papua Pegunungan and Papua Tengah. Consequently, New Guinea's share of AUSTRAL rebounded from a twentieth-century low of 16,9% in 1950 to 30,8% by 2025.

Island Melanesia quadrupled from 527,6k in 1950 to 2,08M in 2025, led by rapid growth in the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu alongside slower, emigration-moderated growth in Fiji (following post-1987 political coups) and New Caledonia. By contrast, Micronesia and Polynesia experienced a distinctive MIRAB demographic equilibrium—combining moderate natural increase with heavy circular and permanent emigration to New Zealand, Australia, the United States and metropolitan France. Reconciled Micronesian totals rose from 180,4k in 1950 to 451,2k in 2000 and plateaued around 458,1k in 2025 (as out-migration from the Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands, Palau and the Northern Marianas balanced high fertility in Kiribati and growth on Guam), while reconciled Polynesian totals climbed from 234,2k in 1950 to 554,1k in 2000 and 624,8k in 2025, with resident populations in Niue, the Cook Islands and Tokelau heavily outnumbered by their diaspora communities in Auckland and Sydney.

  if (yi < 0) paste0(abs(yi), "BC") else if (yi == 0) "1AD" else if (yi <= 1500) paste0(yi, "AD") else as.character(yi)
}

## Pan-Oceanic Metropolitan Hierarchy and Zipf Scaling

AUSTRAL's settlement gazetteer documents one of the sharpest metropolitan-primacy structures of any world macro-region alongside a remarkably clean pan-Oceanic Zipf scaling law once suburban municipalities are properly reconciled (Figure 4 and Table 7). Across 3.412 unique non-suburb localities spanning 25 territories (2.241 in Australia, 625 in New Zealand, 145 in Papua New Guinea, 136 in French Polynesia, 76 in the Federated States of Micronesia, 70 in Indonesian Papua, 47 in Tonga, 46 in Samoa, 44 each in Kiribati and the Marshall Islands, 42 in New Caledonia, 35 in Fiji, 33 in the Solomon Islands, 32 in the Cook Islands, 24 in Vanuatu and 103 across Guam, the Northern Marianas, Palau, Tuvalu, Niue, Wallis and Futuna, Nauru, Rapa Nui, Tokelau and Pitcairn), the upper-tail rank-size distribution ($n = 180$) follows Zipf's law almost identically ($\alpha = 1,09$, $R^2 = 0,996$).

At the apex of the hierarchy sit Oceania's six million-plus metropolitan conurbations, all located in temperate and subtropical Australia and northern New Zealand: Sydney (5,30M), Melbourne (5,06M), Brisbane (2,57M), Perth (2,19M), Auckland (1,62M) and Adelaide (1,40M). Together, these six metropolitan systems concentrate 18,14M inhabitants—more than one-third of the entire 52,09M population of AUSTRAL and over 55% of combined Australian and New Zealand numbers. Immediately below the million-plus tier lies a mixed second tier linking Melanesian primate capitals with secondary Australian and New Zealand coastal and federal hubs: Port Moresby (756,8k), Gold Coast–Tweed Heads (701,9k), Christchurch (510,8k), Newcastle–Maitland (510,2k), Canberra–Queanbeyan (489,2k), Wellington (418,2k), Jayapura (414,9k), Sunshine Coast (387,5k), Wollongong (306,0k), Sorong (295,8k), Geelong (289,6k) and Hobart (250,7k).

```{r fig4-urban, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/04_austral_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Pan-Oceanic metropolitan rank distribution across leading urban agglomerations (Panel A) and log-log Zipf rank-size scaling across 3.412 non-suburb localities (Panel B).",
  "fig:urban-hierarchy"
)
```

Across chapters, Zipf exponents trace the structural evolution of Oceanic urbanism from pre-colonial dispersed village systems to contemporary primate cities. Pre-colonial chapters exhibit flat rank-size slopes ($\alpha = 0,31$ in Pre-Colonial Polynesia, $0,34$ in Pre-European New Zealand, $0,35$ in Pre-Colonial Island Melanesia and Micronesia, and $0,43$ in Pre-1788 Australia), reflecting ecological caps on settlement nucleation where chiefdom centres and seasonal congregations rarely exceeded 2k to 5k persons. Colonial port-capital foundations inverted those slopes sharply upward to $\alpha = 1,26$ in Colonial Australia and $1,27$ in Colonial New Zealand as Sydney, Melbourne and Auckland monopolised maritime trade, rail heads and administrative functions. In the modern era, polycentric coastal urban corridors in Australia moderated its chapter slope to $\alpha = 0,89$, whereas smaller island and highland economies retained steeper primate gradients ($\alpha = 1,23$ in New Zealand, $1,20$ in Modern Island Melanesia and Micronesia, $1,13$ in Modern New Guinea and $1,00$ in Modern Polynesia), anchored by capital port-towns such as Suva, Nouméa, Honiara, Port Vila, Papeete, Apia, Nuku'alofa, South Tarawa and Majuro.

```{r tab-urban, results='asis'}
ts <- root_summary$pan_oceanic_urban_hierarchy$top_settlements
# Filter to non-suburb primary metros and distinct city_proper centres (avoiding duplicate Brisbane/Gold Coast/Canberra/Sunshine Coast/Geelong city_proper rows when parent metro is listed)
skip_dup <- c("Brisbane-Australia", "Gold Coast-Australia", "Canberra-Australia", "Sunshine Coast-Australia", "Greater Geelong-Australia", "Sydney (City)-Australia")
ts_clean <- Filter(function(x) x$population_scope != "suburb" && !(x$key %in% skip_dup), ts)
ts_top <- ts_clean[seq_len(min(15, length(ts_clean)))]

df_urb <- data.frame(
  Rank = seq_along(ts_top),
  Centre = sapply(ts_top, function(x) x$name),
  Territory = sapply(ts_top, function(x) x$country),
  Scope = sapply(ts_top, function(x) if (x$population_scope == "metro") "Metro" else "City proper"),
  Peak_Year = sapply(ts_top, function(x) as.character(x$peak_year)),
  Peak_Pop = sapply(ts_top, function(x) viscount_fmt_pop(x$peak_pop)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_urb) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_urb,
  "Leading reconciled metropolitan agglomerations and primate urban centres across AUSTRAL (excluding subordinate suburban councils and duplicate inner-city cores).",
  c("Rank", "Urban Centre", "Territory", "Scope", "Peak Year", "Peak Pop."),
  list(label = "tab:urban-hierarchy", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Limitations

Four substantive methodological limitations govern interpretation of AUSTRAL's gridded surfaces and tabular trajectories and are documented transparently for downstream demographic and Earth-system users.

First, pre-colonial population envelopes before 1788 remain constrained by taphonomic bias, uneven regional survey intensity and calibration uncertainty between radiocarbon site counts and absolute human headcounts. While institutional archaeological registries in Western Australia, Victoria and Aotearoa New Zealand provide tens of thousands of georeferenced coordinates, coverage across interior Indonesian Papua, parts of the Papua New Guinea Highlands, northern Melanesia and remote coral atolls remains orders of magnitude sparser. The non-stationary Matérn kriging model prevents sparse-survey zones from collapsing to zero through its biophysical trend component, yet absolute pre-contact totals in Australia (784,3k in 1780) and New Guinea (2,20M in 1780) carry unavoidable $\pm 25\%$ to $\pm 35\%$ scholarly uncertainty bands—particularly regarding the timing and spatial reach of early smallpox introductions in late eighteenth-century south-eastern Australia and the pace of post-1600AD sweet-potato demographic expansion in highland New Guinea [@williams2013population; @hunter2015estimating; @denham2024resonating].

Second, a known structural discrepancy exists between 5-arcminute gridded raster sums and reconciled archival census totals across Micronesia and outer Polynesia (Table 6). Because standard 5-arcminute equirectangular cells ($\sim 85\text{ km}^2$ at the equator) under-resolve narrow coral atolls and micro-islands, Micronesia registers zero active terrestrial raster cells on the continental land mask despite holding 458,1k inhabitants in 2025, and outer Polynesian atolls sit partially outside raster coverage (yielding a 769,9k gap between the 52,09M reconciled total and the 51,32M raster sum in 2025). Conversely, prior to 700AD, the unmasked 5-arcminute kriging prior allocates minor background leakage across Aotearoa New Zealand (4,6k to 14,5k) that is explicitly zeroed in the reconciled macro-series to honour radiocarbon arrival chronologies [@burley2012high; @matisoo_smith2026minding]. Analysts performing planetary carbon-cycle or raster-overlay modelling should therefore use the gridded stack for continental and large-island spatial distributions while adopting the reconciled series for exact pan-Oceanic and archipelagic totals.

Third, colonial-era sub-administrative census coverage before 1950 is asymmetrical between settler and tropical jurisdictions. Australia (from 1828–1861) and New Zealand (from 1851) supply dense, decennial colonial and provincial censuses, whereas interior New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and the New Hebrides (Vanuatu) lack comprehensive territorial headcounts prior to the 1966–1971 post-war census round. Even in contemporary Papua New Guinea, the 2024 national census reconciliation and post-2011 administrative splits (Hela, Jiwaka and post-2022 Indonesian Papuan provinces) introduce modest discontinuities between intercensal projections (visible in the 2020–2025 New Guinea plateau from 17,61M to 16,03M) and verified provincial counts.

Fourth, historical boundary transitions between pre-colonial watersheds and colonial administrative colonies—most notably the 1780–1800 shift in Australia where Indigenous contact collapse overlaps with the transition from 11 pre-1788 watershed polygons to the two-colony 1800 New South Wales and New Holland geometry—require careful reading across chapter seams. Readers investigating sub-regional dynamics during transitional decades should consult the paired colonial and pre-colonial chapter monographs directly (Chapters 1 through 11), which tabulate every underlying archival estimate and regional boundary definition individually.

# Conclusion

AUSTRAL delivers a unified, bottom-up historical spatial-demographic synthesis across Australia, New Zealand, New Guinea, Island Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia (excluding Hawai'i and American Samoa) spanning 10000BC to 2025. By integrating 16 chronological and regional monographs, 310 open-access scholarly studies, 69.018 primary institutional archaeological records with zero crowd-sourced fallback, non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across eight Holocene horizons, 14 strictly non-anachronistic historical GIS boundary regimes across all 118 Common Era epochs (mass-conservation error $\le 4,44 \times 10^{-8}$), and 3.763 coordinate-anchored settlement trajectories disciplined by three-phase metropolitan reconciliation, AUSTRAL overcomes the chief limitations of backward-projected sovereign baselines across Oceania.

From 236,4k hunter-gatherers and early highland foragers in 10000BC through the independent Kuk Swamp agricultural revolution, the Lapita and Polynesian oceanic expansions, the 3,81M pre-contact crest around 1780, the 3,29M colonial epidemic nadir of 1820 and the twentieth-century rise to 52,09M inhabitants anchored by a tightly fitted Zipf urban hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,09$, $R^2 = 0,996$), the reconstruction captures the deep ecological and historical diversity of the Pacific world. Pixel-exact seam exclusions against Southeast Asia, Hawai'i and the Pacific rim prepare all AUSTRAL rasters, settlement gazetteers and macro-series for direct planetary compositing.

# Appendix

All 16 constituent chapters of AUSTRAL are organised into three chronological series: Pre-Colonial Oceania (Chapters 1 to 5: Pre-1788 Aboriginal Australia and Tasmania; Pre-Colonial New Guinea and Bismarck Archipelago; Pre-Colonial Island Melanesia and Micronesia; Pre-Colonial Polynesia; and Pre-European New Zealand), Colonial Oceania (Chapters 6 to 11: Colonial Australia from First Fleet to Federation; Colonial New Zealand; Colonial New Guinea; Colonial Island Melanesia; Colonial Micronesia; and Colonial Polynesia), and Modern Oceania (Chapters 12 to 16: Commonwealth of Australia after 1901; New Zealand after 1907; Papua New Guinea and Indonesian Papua; Modern Island Melanesia and Micronesia; and Polynesia in the Modern Era). Each chapter module contains a literature review monograph, an evidence-only settlement gazetteer report, machine-readable settlement trajectories, a 4320x2160 areal mask, a matched vector partition, a source saturation ledger, visual inspection manifests and an archival library of 18 to 20 open-access scholarly PDFs. Machine-readable root diagnostics, pan-Oceanic Zipf tables, eight-horizon Matérn variogram parameters and reconciled macro-series are archived alongside this synthesis in the shared summary registry.

Note 1. Throughout AUSTRAL, Hawai'i, Palmyra Atoll and American Samoa are assigned to the neighbouring North American and Central Pacific CENTAUR domain, while Maluku (including Seram, Halmahera, Kai and Aru) is assigned to the Southeast Asian MANDALA domain; Raja Ampat and the entire island of New Guinea remain unified inside AUSTRAL to preserve biogeographic and ethnographic continuity across Sahul.

Note 2. Numerical conventions follow European decimal commas (58,88), full-stop thousands grouping (69.018), semantic magnitude suffixes (k and M) and non-Oxford British English spelling. Pre-Common Era dates omit thousands punctuation (10000BC), while Common Era benchmarks through 1500AD carry attached AD suffixes (1AD, 1000AD, 1500AD).

Note 3. Dual reporting of reconciled pan-Oceanic totals (52,09M in 2025) alongside 5-arcminute continental-insular raster sums (51,32M in 2025) preserves exact accounting for sub-pixel Micronesian and Polynesian coral atolls without artificially inflating neighbouring pelagic cells or distorting large-island population densities.

Note 4. Three-phase metropolitan reconciliation separates metropolitan statistical areas (55 units), standalone cities and towns (3.357 units) and subordinate suburban councils (351 units) so that Australian and New Zealand outer-suburban local government areas remain available for intra-urban research while avoiding rank-size distortion in pan-Oceanic Zipf regressions.
